title: ‘Adam’s Law’ Enjoys Early TV-Ratings Judgment at CBS
description:
Adam Levy usually delivers verdicts, but he probably doesn’t mind receiving this one.

	His syndicated program, “Adam’s Law” is the most-watched ne
body:
Adam Levy usually delivers verdicts, but he probably doesn’t mind receiving this one.

	His syndicated program, “Adam’s Law” is the most-watched new series in the category so far in the 2026-2027 TV season, according to data from Nielsen. During the week of October 19, the program hit a new high in viewership, capturing an average audience of 1.33 million. Season to date, the program is luring an average of 1.29 million viewers.
	

	Levy and his backer, CBS, bet they could replace the hit “Judge Judy,” a daytime-TV mainstay that ran on TV for 25 years. For Levy, that’s no small task. Judy Sheindlin, the star of that program, is his mother.

	Viewers were “being asked to simply tune in to my show because of who my mother was, because of who I was related to,” Levy says during a recent interview. “There were many who were hesitant, who thought that this was a gimmick.”

	Now, after being on the air for several weeks, he hopes the audience is impressed by what he brings to the screen. Levy makes sure to explore whether litigants on the program have past history with the court or an established record of making frivolous claims.

	“This is what judges should be doing. Judges should be holding people’s feet to the fire,” Levy says. He believes TV audiences appreciate seeing him do the extra work and holding people to account. If judges “chastised lawyers when they came in and made what are outright, just complete lies,” they would face less frivolous litigation, Levy says.

	Levy has a long history with the law. He served as an actual district attorney and assistant district attorney, and later became one of the judges on the Amazon Prime Video series, “Tribunal Justice.”
	

	CBS is also tracking Levy’s social-media following. So far, he’s nabbed 321,000 followers on Instagram, 214,000 on Facebook, 33,000 on TikTok and 30,000 on YouTUbe. Levy suggests that he’s only getting started. “I see this show going on for quite a number of years,” he says. 

	“I hope this starts a movement,” he says of response to his techniques, “and that we start getting better judges as a result.”

title: From Startup to Stand-Up: A Former Tech Founder Wanted to Pursue Comedy — So He Sold Shares in His Career
description: It was just like any other pitch to investors: justify the valuation, address the risks and make lots of impressive-looking pie charts and graphs.
body:
It was just like any other pitch to investors: justify the valuation, address the risks and make lots of impressive-looking pie charts and graphs. Except this time, Pete McEntegart wasn’t raising money for a tech startup, he was selling shares of himself.

	The 57-year-old North Carolinian had tried his hand as a Goldman Sachs investment banker, Sports Illustrated columnist and startup co-founder. But a few years ago, on Christmas Day, he had a bit of an epiphany. “I was on a run, and I realized I wanted to take one more big swing before I got too old,” he tells Variety. He decided it was time to pursue a career in stand-up comedy. Pete McEntegart was no more; from that day forward, he’d be known as Pete Smack.
	

	It doesn’t take a business genius to realize joke telling is not the easiest way to make a buck. And, as with startups, it takes a while for many comics to turn a profit — if a profit is to be turned at all. So, Smack decided he would raise money for his comedic venture and hold himself accountable to investors.

	He turned to the startup crowdfunding service Wefunder and became the first entertainer to solicit investors on the platform. By early last year, he raised nearly $60,000 from 104 investors, the majority of whom committed between $100 and $150. Buying into Smack is a legitimate investment regulated by the SEC. To set up his seed round, so to speak, the comedian spent $5,000 on lawyers.

	Smack pitched prospective investors in a humorous presentation posted to his Wefunder page. “You can’t have a truly diversified portfolio if you’re not directly invested in a standup comedian,” he began.
	



	

									Courtesy of Pete Smack
	



	Smack offered family, friends and strangers on the internet a chance to split 10% of his gross revenues through 2029. On Jan. 1, 2030, their investment converts to equity at a $1 million pre-money valuation. “While I can’t guarantee what your financial return will be — the lawyers were pretty adamant about that,” Smack wrote on his Wefunder page, “I’m confident you’ll have a fun and entertainingly documented ride.”

	In detail, Smack laid out how he plans to deliver a return for his investors. He’ll focus on corporate gigs and cruise ships, as well as “55 and greater” active-living communities. Plus, he’s a clean comic, and as he wrote in the pitch, “CLEAN = GREEN ($$$).”

	Smack also provides projections of what the investors’ collective share of his revenue might look like through 2029, with his conservative estimate at $55,000, upside case at $116,500 and dream case at $228,000. Some of his data is less quantitative.



	

									Courtesy of Pete Smack
	



	Smack’s history with stand-up comedy started in the 1990s, when he began writing sitcom scripts after college and before his stint at Goldman Sachs. For a “Seinfeld” spec, he had to write some stand-up material for Jerry, and he realized it came naturally to him. In 1996, Smack signed up for an open mic in Virginia, but nobody showed up, so the event was canceled.

	“I went home and performed for my two roommates,” Smack says. “I used a ping-pong paddle as a microphone.”

	Nearly a decade later, when Smack was living in New York and writing for Sports Illustrated, he took a comedy class and participated in a showcase at the end of it. But he had never given stand-up a real shot. Now, he’s convinced he can succeed at it.

	So far, Smack has used his seed money to rent out a venue and film a special, “Last Man Standing,” which debuted on Sept. 22 on VOD platforms via Comedy Dynamics. He thinks the money can last him a few years; he’s able to keep his costs low, in part, because after his dad died in 2024, he moved in with his mom. “I’m figuring out how to make this work — as a living and as a business,” he says.



	

									Courtesy of Pete Smack
	



	Smack sends a monthly newsletter updating investors on his progress. But any pressure he feels is mostly self-imposed. “If they make money, they’ll be excited,” Smack says of his backers, “but they just want to be along for the ride.” According to a six-page annual report, Smack brought in $18,497 in revenue in 2025 and had $9,585 in expenses. He says 2026 is on a similar pace.
	

	He’s hoping a streamer licenses his special, and he’s writing a TV pilot loosely based on his life. He’s also exploring creative sources of cash, like speaking to corporate audiences about how lessons from stand-up can translate to business success. He filmed a TEDx talk that has yet to come out, and he’s working on a new hour that he dreams of taking to the Edinburgh Fringe. In his October newsletter, he floated some title ideas to his investors.

	“The new show has the working title ‘A Happy Schmedium,’” he wrote. “(Other contenders: ‘Time Flies,’ ‘Time Flew’ and ‘Time Is a Fat Circle.’) The broad theme is the passage of time.”

	He thinks the progress reports help his supporters feel, well, invested in his career. “You know,” Smack says, “because they literally are.”

title: ‘Bad Day’ Trailer: Cameron Diaz Is a Single Mom Who Accidentally Robs a Bank in Netflix Comedy
description: A towed car, frozen bank account and passive-aggressive comments from gossiping pilates moms are just a few of the unfortunate events that happen t
body:
A towed car, frozen bank account and passive-aggressive comments from gossiping pilates moms are just a few of the unfortunate events that happen to Cameron Diaz in Netflix’s “Bad Day” trailer.

	The “big-heart mom-com” film, which hits the streamer on Dec. 11, gives a glimpse of just how bad this day will get in its new trailer. Diaz plays a single mom of two daughters who pinky-promised to make an appearance at her youngest child’s soccer game, but the universe has other plans for her. Whether it’s taking her father to his dialysis appointment or proving her innocence in bank fraud, something always seems to get in the way of her keeping her promise.
	

	“Bad Day” blends Diaz’s “Back in Action” and “Charlie’s Angels” action experience with her heartfelt roles like “There’s Something About Mary” and “The Holiday.” Joining her are Danielle Brooks (“Orange Is the New Black”) and John Higgins as a pair of police officers, Ed O’Neill as her father, Rhenzy Feliz (“The Penguin”) as her friend, along with Emma Pearson and Jessica Belkin as her daughters. Mark Duplass, Jessica Belkin, Rob Corddry, Ayden Mayeri, Ben Schwartz, Retta, Emma Pearson, P.J. Byrne, Sherry Cola, Edi Patterson and Beck Bennett are also among the cast.

	The movie is directed by Jake Szymanski, who helmed the Amazon Prime Video series “Jury Duty.” Laura Solon is the writer, and Beau Bauman is a producer. Mark Moran and Laura Solon are executive producers, with Jeremy Mittleman serving as a co-producer.

	Watch the full trailer below.

title: ‘Jet Lag: The Game’ Heads to Movie Theaters Across US, UK and Canada for Season 20 ‘Hide and Seek: Italy’ Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)

	In partnership wit
body:
Nebula original series “Jet Lag: The Game” is heading back to movie theaters for the travel competition’s Season 20 premiere. 

	In partnership with Regal, Picturehouse, Cineworld and Landmark Cinemas across the U.S., U.K., and Canada, the 90-minute premiere of “Jet Lag: The Game” Season 20 “Hide + Seek: Italy” will screen across more than 160 theatre screens in three countries on Dec. 5. Tickets for the event go on sale today, Nov. 5.
	

	The upcoming event marks the largest international theatrical release for the series to date following the Season 19 “Japanorama” premiere screening in August at Picturehouse Cinemas in London and the later international rollout of the Season 19 finale across Regal, Picturehouse and Cineworld locations in October. 

	Select theaters will feature an on-screen trivia experience ahead of the “Jet Lag: The Game” Season 2 premiere screening.

	One of indie streamer Nebula’s most popular original series, “Jet Lag: The Game” has featured competitions across Japan, New Zealand, Europe, Australia, and North America throughout its first 19 seasons. “Jet Lag: The Game” stars the show’s creators Sam Denby, Ben Doyle and Adam Chase along with a rotating cast of guest competitors.

	Per Nebula’s description for the new season, “In ‘Hide + Seek: Italy,’ the 20th season of Jet Lag: The Game, the boys face off in a six-day game of Hide + Seek across Italy, exploring its scenic seaside towns, medieval mountain villages and rolling Roman hills. But this season is no vacation: the classic Hide + Seek format has been elevated to ‘Expert Mode,’ removing the game’s most powerful questions and introducing new mechanics designed to punish seekers for making mistakes. In the season premiere, Ben and Adam grapple with the new Expert Mode questions as Sam relaxes on the beach.”
	

	“The magic of ‘Jet Lag’ is the community, so it’s a real joy to work with our friends at Picturehouse, Regal, Cineworld, and Landmark to bring that community together in the real world,” Nebula founder Dave Wiskus said.

	“Our first Jet Lag: The Game theatrical event demonstrated the potential of bringing an established digital audience into the movie theatre,” Regal senior vice president of U.S. content Brooks LeBoeuf said. “Nebula has built one of the most engaged fanbases in the creator space, and that enthusiasm translated directly into theatrical demand. ‘Hide + Seek Italy’ builds on that momentum, and we look forward to welcoming fans back to experience the series together on the big screen.”

title: ‘Wednesday’ Director Paco Cabezas and Javier Ruiz Caldera, Helmer of ‘5 More Minutes,’ Talk Genre Filmmaking and Creative Risk
description: Spanish directors Paco Cabezas and Javier Ruiz Caldera compared notes on demanding shoots and creative risk at this year’s South International Seri
body:
Spanish directors Paco Cabezas and Javier Ruiz Caldera compared notes on demanding shoots and creative risk at this year’s South International Series Festival in Cádiz.

	Their Nov. 2 conversation, “No Holds Barred,” was part of the festival’s Creative Talks program, moderated by South Boost coordinator Alejandro Ávila. South’s fourth edition ran Oct. 30-Nov. 4.

	Cabezas, whose credits range from Netflix’s “Wednesday” to AMC’s “The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon,” summed up the pressure of the job: “I’ve always compared shooting to painting a picture during a fire or writing a poem on a roller coaster.”
	

	Before each shoot, he assembles a thick book of drawings, photographs and shot breakdowns. By the time he gets to set, he knows it so well he barely opens it.

	“To create under pressure, you have to be very relaxed,” Cabezas said.

	Ruiz Caldera favors leaving some things to chance: “Leave the window open so the air can come in and things can happen.”

	He has  carved out a career from taking comedy into unfamiliar territory, from spy caper “Anacleto: Agente Secreto” to superhero romp “Superlópez.” Horror, he confessed, is actually his favorite genre. “As soon as I run out of adjectives to put before comedy, I’ll make a big drama,” he joked.

	After last year’s family drama “Wolfgang,” Ruiz Caldera changed direction again. “5 More Minutes” (“5 Minutos Más”), written by Berto Romero and starring Romero, Belén Cuesta and Javier Cámara, is a time-loop thriller shot in continuous takes of exactly five minutes.
	

	Even a take running six seconds over meant starting again. Finishing early required finding a pause to fill the remaining time.

	“I think it’s been the wildest technical challenge of my life,” said Ruiz Caldera, who came to filmmaking through editing. “Editing is possibly my favorite filmmaking tool,” he added. For this film, “I took that tool away from myself.”

	Produced by El Terrat and Ikiru Films as a Movistar Plus original, “5 More Minutes” premiered in competition at San Sebastián, where Cámara won the Silver Shell for best supporting performance. The film also earned the coveted Audience Award and a Special Jury Mention at Austin’s Fantastic Fest. Filmax handles international sales and will release the movie in Spain Jan. 22.

	Ruiz Caldera wanted Romero in the lead, although the comedian worried that viewers would expect jokes from a screenplay containing almost none. The director felt Romero’s presence would bring humor to the film even without conventional comic dialogue.

	“I think humor is an essential ingredient if you want to move people more, or scare them more,” he said.

	Cabezas put it another way. “If you laugh with someone, you love them more,” he said. “So when you put them in danger, you suffer more.”

	Ruiz Caldera sees a similar connection between comedy and horror, provided the frightening moments are played straight. “The key is to take horror seriously,” he said. There is also a danger in pushing the humor too far: “A bad joke can ruin a film.”

	When Ávila brought up action choreography, Cabezas grinned. “I’ve killed a lot of people in fiction,” he said.

	His example came from “The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon,” where a catapult launches a giant flaming ball made of zombies toward the heroes. Reading the script, Cabezas wondered: “How do I make a giant meatball of burning zombies explode against the heroes?”

	The solution involved a van rigged to jolt on cue, a drone carrying a light to trace the incoming fireball and stunt performers attached to a constructed ball who broke away on impact.

	“If I’ve already done a giant flaming meatball made of zombies, what else can I do?” he asked, laughing.

	Cabezas said he had shot equally “crazy” material for the upcoming third season of “Wednesday,” though spoilers were off-limits.
	

	His Spanish TV work has featured Atresplayer’s admired “La Novia Gitana” crime saga, most recently “La Nena,” a co-production between Banijay Iberia’s Diagonal and Buendía Estudios Canarias for Atresmedia. Cabezas described the “total freedom” he enjoyed on that project, compared with the established visual parameters of a show such as “Wednesday.”

	Asked about working in Spain and the U.S., he acknowledged the differences in resources without drawing a wider cultural divide. “There are differences in budgets, but in the end the heart is the same.”

	The directors first worked together on the 2009 spoof “Spanish Movie,” written by Cabezas and directed by Ruiz Caldera in his feature debut.

	“Possibly the best day I’ve ever had on a shoot was on ‘Spanish Movie,’” Ruiz Caldera recalled. That was when he brought Leslie Nielsen and Spanish comedy star Chiquito de la Calzada together in front of two hidden cameras for the Telecinco Cinema–Think Studio production.

	Ruiz Caldera asked Nielsen to imitate Chiquito, then let the two comedians improvise. Watching them was “like a National Geographic of comedy,” he said.

	Cabezas’ Hollywood career began after his thriller “Neon Flesh” (“Carne de Neón”) reached Tribeca. Meetings in Los Angeles led to Nicolas Cage film “Rage” and U.S. TV assignments.

	Yet when an audience member asked about the biggest challenge of his career, Cabezas went further back, to the short film that preceded “Neon Flesh.”

	At a private screening, a producer declared it unfunny and refused to pay to transfer the digitally shot film to celluloid for festival screenings. Cabezas raised €10,000 ($11,200) from relatives, became a co-producer and financed the transfer himself.

	At its first festival screening, the audience laughed. The short went on to win 60 awards, he recalled.

	The hardest part, Cabezas said, had been “believing in yourself and taking that risk.”

title: Rhys Ifans on the ‘Frightening’ Task of Portraying Parkinson’s in ‘Onwards and Sideways’ and Learning to Wear ‘Costume’ of Disease: ‘I Really Did My Homework’
description: Less than a year after “I Swear” helped explain the complexities of Tourette’s Syndrome on the big screen, “Onwards and Sideways” is looking to do
body:
Less than a year after “I Swear” helped explain the complexities of Tourette’s Syndrome on the big screen, “Onwards and Sideways” is looking to do the same for Parkinson’s Disease.

	From director John Madden (“Shakespeare in Love”) and written by Paul Mayhew-Archer (who was diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 2011), the film — released in U.K. cinemas on Friday — stars Welsh screen legend Rhys Ifans as Tony, a much-loved and deeply caring primary school teacher who is calmly told by a doctor he has “five good years” left before Parkinson’s takes over his life. At almost the same time and at the same clinic, musician Emma (Laura Linney) is given the same diagnoses, and the story follows the journey of the pair as they try to manage and come to terms with a disease that, as they’re both painfully aware, is only going to get worse. 
	

	Like “I Swear” before it, “Onwards and Sideways” is a film that’s deeply moving, at times upsetting to watch but frequently funny, and also one that brings to light various aspects of an incurable disorder that most viewers probably knew very little about. As it shows, among the various side-effects of the drugs used to help manage Parkinson’s is compulsive spending and gambling. 

	For Ifans, known for playing Hugh Grant’s raucous housemate in “Notting Hill,” but also for “Mr Nice,” “Not Only But Always” (which saw him win a BAFTA TV award for playing Peter Cook) and numerous other screen and stage roles over a career spanning 30 years, the film — and working so closely with the “heaven-sent” Linney — was unlike anything he’d experienced before. 
	

	But, as he explains to Variety, it was also one that came with a deep responsibility to accurately portray a disease that people around the world live with each day. From “consuming everything” he could about the neurological disorder to attending a dance class with sufferers, Ifans details how he learned to “wear the Parkinson’s costume.”
	
		When a script like that lands on your desk, one written so exquisitely about such a sensitive subject, what’s your immediate response?	

	As an actor, it’s the perfect list: tender, dark, funny, moving, complicated and nuanced. That’s life. I always respond well to anything where laughter and tears are often dancing together.
	
		Preparing for a role like this must have required more care and responsibility than others.	

	We were representing a vast worldwide demographic of people who live with Parkinson’s day by day, and will live with it for the rest of their lives. It’s something that won’t get better — it evolves. So there was no question that we had to do everything in our power to make the portrayal as authentic, real and tangible as possible. Laura and I both went to great lengths, consuming everything we could about Parkinson’s. 

	There’s a wonderful podcast called “Movers and Shakers,” which our writer, Paul Mayhew-Archer, is part of. I devoured their entire back catalogue, driving the length and breadth of England and Wales while listening to the experiences of people living with Parkinson’s. I learned about everything, from how to get dressed to coping with sleep, and all the little details in between.

	On the physical side, our director John Madden brought in two wonderful women, Laura and Anna, from a group called Neuro Heroes. They’re neurophysiotherapists who work closely with the Parkinson’s community and people with other neurological conditions, helping them understand their bodies and the importance of exercise. They worked with us for two or three weeks before filming began. We mapped it all out and it was daunting and frightening. Both Laura and I wanted to run away. But slowly, it starts to fit. You begin to wear the Parkinson’s costume, if you like, and it starts to feel as though it belongs to you, as much as it can for someone who isn’t living with it every day.

	Of course, I’ll never get close to understanding what it truly feels like. The words I’ve heard from people who have Parkinson’s are that you’re constantly under attack from your own body, under siege in many ways. But we had to do our best. So, to give you the short answer: I really did my homework.
	
	
		I think I read that you also joined a dance class?	

	Yes. Laura went to some wonderful classes in Juilliard, where people with Parkinson’s move to music. It gives them some respite from their symptoms. Something happens neurologically when music reaches the brain; it almost hacks into your system and gives you a sense of levity.

	I went to a wonderful class in North Wales. These classes take place all over the world, with people with Parkinson’s gathering in church halls, ballet studios and other spaces. The one in Wales was particularly close to my heart because, of course, I’m Welsh. But it was an amazing collection of people, both those running the class and those attending. There was a harpist and even a support dog.

	It’s incredible to watch a room full of people with Parkinson’s enter, seemingly shackled by their condition, and then see what music and community can do for their minds and bodies. It’s incredibly powerful.
	
		This film is about much more than the disease and what it does to you — it’s also about that community.	

	Absolutely. I wouldn’t call it a love story. I’d call it a story about love. And that love is spread far and wide.
	
		That wonderful moment at the end with the children in the school saying goodbye to Tony is so moving. I don’t think it’s possible not to cry during that scene.	

	For me, that’s the moment when I’m fully kebabed by the film. From then on, it’s very difficult to stay in control. It’s a wonderful moment. 

	My father was a primary school teacher, and I remember his final day at school. I really got a sense of how it must have felt for him. I really wanted to play the best teacher I could. So, for me, the film is twofold: it’s an homage to the courage of people with Parkinson’s, but equally an homage to great teachers.
	
		Parkinson’s is a disease that I don’t think many people really understand. Watching the film, I realized just how little I knew. I had ignorantly assumed it was simply a matter of having the shakes, but I had no idea about the range of neurological symptoms and side-effects, including things like gambling addiction.	

	There are up to 40 Parkinson’s symptoms. And counting, probably. Everyone gets their own version of the disease. Of course, there’s the symptom we’re all familiar with: shaking. But my character, Tony, doesn’t shake. He experiences a phenomenon where he freezes and is unable to move forward. Then there are the medications that ease these symptoms, but they often come with very strange and disturbing side effects. These can range from gambling and sex addiction to constipation.
	

	That’s a whole other universe that people with Parkinson’s have to navigate, juggle and come to terms with. I think the film really explores that part of a Parkinson’s sufferer’s daily life, including the whole ritual of taking medication at the right time. You’re constantly trying to stay on top of symptoms that could literally floor you.
	
		We’ve had a few beautiful, tender, real and also funny films over the past year about conditions and illnesses that people didn’t always necessarily understand. “I Swear” last year was phenomenal, and now there’s “Elsinore” and this. It feels like there’s a real moment in cinema of films looking to help explain diseases we thought we knew about, but actually don’t.	

	I think film is a great way of introducing people to these subjects. There’s a line in the film: “You need to know the person behind the symptoms.” Film does that better than almost any other medium because it potentially reaches so many people. 

	Everyone I’ve spoken to who has seen the film has walked out of the cinema knowing or understanding more about Parkinson’s. For me, that’s job done.
	
		Of course, your scenes with the wonderful Laura (Linney) are fantastic, but I also loved seeing Monica (Dolan). She’s on a real roll at the moment and appearing in so many brilliant films, including “Elsinore.”	

	Laura is literally heaven-sent. I wouldn’t have been able to achieve what we’ve achieved here without Laura and me being able to make ourselves completely available to each other in a way I’ve never experienced before. We had to be able to say to each other, very early on, how frightened we were about entering into this. Laura has been wonderful. 

	And then Monica is like the cavalry. There are actors like that: you call on them, they come in and they deliver every time. She’s a master craftswoman. She has the most exquisite timing, humanity and authenticity. I really felt I was in the company of two very special women in this film, between her and Laura. It was a pleasure coming to work every day.
	
		You and Laura hadn’t previously starred alongside each other, but you’ve both appeared in beloved Richard Curtis romantic comedies. Did you discuss your experiences on “Notting Hill” and “Love Actually” at all?	

	Funnily enough, while we were rehearsing, Richard came and had lunch with us one afternoon. He’s very nosy and wanted to know what we were up to. I describe Richard as Christmas in trousers. He’s a wonderful being. Laura and I would often regale ourselves with fondness and love for Richard. He’s never too far away, and, of course, he was a great friend and collaborator of Paul Mayhew-Archer, who wrote the script. So, yes, Richard was spoken of often and fondly.
	

	See the “Onwards and Sideways” trailer below:

schema.headline: Rhys Ifans on the ‘Frightening’ Task of Portraying Parkinson’s in ‘Onwards and Sideways’ and Learning to Wear ‘Costume’ of Disease: ‘I Really Did My Homework’

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Takes Imax to Biggest Quarterly Revenue to Date
description:
After a record-breaking summer season, Imax swung to its best-ever revenue and profits for the third quarter of 2026.

	Fueled by Christopher Nolan
body:
After a record-breaking summer season, Imax swung to its best-ever revenue and profits for the third quarter of 2026.

	Fueled by Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” the company’s highest grossing release of all time, Imax logged $175 million in revenue during Q3, up 64% from the $106.7 million reported in the same three-month period in 2025. Imax reported a net income of $117.1 million, a staggering 400% increase from $22.6 million a year earlier. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings per share rose to $2.21, up 370% from 47 cents in the comparable year-ago period.
	

	As the industry enjoyed the biggest summer in post-pandemic times, Imax’s worldwide box office tally for Q3 stood at $712 million, towering 94% above the $368 million posted a year ago. On Imax screens, “The Odyssey” alone surpassed $550 million worldwide in the three-month period — representing 30% of the movie’s staggering $1.8 billion total haul. Those ticket sales crushed the company’s prior record-holder, 2009’s “Avatar,” with $271 million, not adjusted for inflation.

	“The Odyssey” was a juggernaut on the company’s screens in part because it was the first feature shot entirely with Imax film cameras. (Other tentpoles have incorporated Imax’s technology for select sequences.) This quarter’s other top-earning titles for Imax were “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “Resident Evil” and “Avengers Endgame Encore.”

	“What Imax achieved goes beyond simply a ‘great quarter’ and transcends the many records we shattered in the period,” said Rich Gelfond, CEO of Imax. ”What we believe we are witnessing is an awakening to the power and potential of our platform to impact global culture, unlock new commercial opportunities, and inspire a new level of demand and awe in audiences around the world.”
	

	Imax has been a true commercial draw in recent years, with audiences gravitating toward the big and bright screens to distinguish from the experience of watching a movie from the couch. Given the increased consumer demand, Imax continues to to expand its global footprint, signings agreements for over 100 systems worldwide to date in 2026 — 65% of which are for new locations. With blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday” (which is only playing in Imax in China) on schedule in December, Imax expects to exceed earlier projections of $1.4 billion in 2026. Last year, the company set a new record with $1.2 billion globally. 

	“We are excited for the year ahead and confident in our belief that there has never been a better time to be in the Imax business. This ‘Imax awakening’ sits inside a bigger culture shift of people around the world — particularly young people — seeking connection, community, and shared experiences that feel bigger than any one person’s screen,” Gelfond said. “Imax has always delivered these moments, and we believe this trend has only begun to benefit our business.”

schema.headline: ‘The Odyssey’ Takes Imax to Biggest Quarterly Revenue to Date

title: Russell Brand Found Guilty of Rape and Sexual Assault at London Trial; Taken Into Custody
description: Russell Brand, the former actor and comedian, was convicted Thursday on three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape in his London criminal
body:
Russell Brand, the former actor and comedian, was convicted Thursday on three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape in his London criminal trial. He was found not guilty of two other rape charges and a count of attempted indecent assault.

	The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, informed Brand that “obviously a custodial sentence of some length will result” and said it was unlikely he would extend the former comedian’s bail any further.
	

	“You’ve been convicted of a number of offenses, including one of rape,” he said. “My current view is that I therefore have to remand you in custody not least because the temptation to avoid coming back to court to receive that sentence will be overwhelming.”

	He allowed both Brand’s legal team and the Crown Prosecution Service a break of 20 minutes before returning to make submissions as to whether bail should be extended. Ultimately, however, the judge denied the application to extend bail and remanded him into custody until Monday, when he will return to receive his sentence. As Brand was taken to the cells, he mouthed “I’m OK” and “I’m good” to his lawyers and gave a thumbs-up sign, according to Sky News.

	In the U.K., a rape conviction can result in up to 19 years in prison and potentially even a life sentence, depending on the seriousness of the offense. The maximum sentence for sexual assault is 10 years.

	Sky News reported that the Met Police are now investigating further allegations of rape made by two women.

	Brand did not visibly react when the verdicts were read out. His wife, Laura Gallacher, rushed out of the courtroom when Brand was taken to the cells to wait before his bail application.
	

	Brand was accused of raping three women at various locations between 1999 and 2009. One of the alleged victims also accused him of sexual assault in addition to oral rape. He was also accused of one count of attempted indecent assault at MTV’s U.K. offices in 2001 and one count of sexual assault in 2009.

	The jury was on its third day of deliberations when it reached the verdict, following a three-week trial.

	Brand got his start as a comedian on MTV in the U.K. before rising through the ranks of British media to host shows such as “Big Brother” spin-off ” Big Brother’s Big Mouth” on Channel 4 network E4 and his own radio show, “The Russell Brand Show” on BBC Radio 6.

	He then broke through in Hollywood after appearing in the 2007 comedy “St Trinian’s” starring Talulah Riley, Juno Temple and Colin Firth, set in a girls’ boarding school. Roles in “Forgetting Sarah Marshall,” “Get Him to the Greek” and “Rock of Ages.” He also voiced a recurring character in the “Despicable Me” franchise, Dr Nefario.

	He eventually launched his own podcast and moved into influencing and politics via his YouTube channel.

	However his media empire came crashing down in 2023 when The Sunday Times of London and Channel 4 documentary series “Dispatches” published/broadcast a joint investigation into Brand’s allegedly predatory behaviour, in which five women accused Brand of sexual assault and misconduct.

schema.headline: Russell Brand Found Guilty of Rape and Sexual Assault at London Trial; Taken Into Custody

title: ‘Rings of Power’ Star Eddie Marsan on Playing a Power-Hungry Dwarf and Why He Once Had 2,000 Pairs of Orlando Bloom’s Elf Ears in His Attic
description:
There’s political upheaval in Khazad-dûm.

	Following the seismic events that shook the Dwarven underground kingdom in “The Lord of the Rings: The
body:
There’s political upheaval in Khazad-dûm.

	Following the seismic events that shook the Dwarven underground kingdom in “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” season 2 finale, which saw King Durin III sacrifice himself in order to deal with an unruly Balrog he’d accidentally awoken, Prince Durin IV was anointed his successor. But in step Thrain, Durin III’s older son — and technically the rightful heir — to challenge for the crown, sparking a major power struggle and fallout.
	

	Played by veteran British actor Eddie Marsan, Thrain is one of the most notable new additions in the third season of show, which launches Nov. 11 on Prime Video. And while it may be Marsan’s first on-screen adventure into Middle-earth, he’s no stranger to Tolkien’s world. As it happens, “The Lord of the Rings” has been a major part of his family’s life for more than two decades — to the extent he once had several thousand pairs of Orlando Blooms prosthetic Elven ears stored in his house.

	Speaking to Variety, Marsan explains his meditation routine during the lengthy make-up process and why he only joined the show to take the piss out his friend Peter Mullan.
	
		But how did it feel joining ‘Rings of Power’ and like donning the armor of Thrain and and the dwarves deep down beneath the mountains?	

	It kind of felt slightly inevitable, really. My wife Janine [Schneider-Marsan] was a makeup artist on the original Lord of the Rings film. So I was shooting “Gangs of New York” and flew out to see her in New Zealand, and we spent some time together. And she kept going back for years afterwards to do the sequels and  do pickups. So it was part of our early marriage for three or four years.
	
	
		That’s fantastic.	

	She did the makeup for Orlando Bloom and Liv Tyler. And in our old house, in the loft, we had around 2,000 pairs of Orlando Bloom’s ears.
	
		What do you do with 2000 pairs of Orlando Bloom’s ears?	

	I was going to bring them to “Rings and Powers” to see if they wanted them! But it was all part of our family life. And I also watched the show, because Peter Mullan is a very good friend, and I really loved the end of the second series when he sacrifices himself. I thought it was incredible. And then they came in and said, “Would you like to play Peter’s son?” And it was two things. I wanted to do it because I thought the show was brilliant, the writing was great, the direction was great. I thought the action was amazing. But also to be able to take the piss out of Peter and tell him that I’m playing his son.
	
		Ha! How did he take to that? 	

	He didn’t take it too kindly.
	
		So was it a straight yes when the offer came in?	

	Yes.  I mean, I look like a dwarf. But no, it was a straight yes. I wanted to do it. I knew that Peter had done it and Rory [Kinnear] had done it, and I admired their work in it and I was a fan of the show. Also, I love to mix things up. I love to do something that’s completely different to what I’ve done before. I have very little control over other aspects of my career, like whether you’re going to be in fashion or not, whether you’re going to be the hot new thing or not. All that comes in and out. You’ve got no control over that, but what you can control is the content — whether I always do something that’s completely different to what I’ve done before. So I came out of “Rings of Power.” Then we shot the second series of Netflix’s “Supercell.” Then Netflix asked me to be J. Edgar Hoover in “Kennedy,” which I did. So my approach to it all is to mix it up as much as possible. That’s what I enjoy.
	
		You’re you’re playing Thrain. How would you describe him and how he fits into that sort of complex politics of the Dwarven kingdom?	

	Well, he’s the eldest brother of Durin the fourth, played by Owain [Arthur], and he’s the eldest son of Durin the Third, which is Peter Mullins’ character. And he was overlooked. He feels like he should have been the king. And his younger brother, was made the king. So in many ways, he’s kind of like Fredo in “The Godfather.” So at the beginning of episode three, he comes back to Khazad-dûm to kind of reclaim his crown.
	
	
		Did you dig deep into Thrain’s timeline and history? He doesn’t make it to the ‘Lord of the Rings’ films, but I think there’s a there’s a deleted scene in ‘The Hobbit’ films that he’s seen in.	

	They gave me a a kind of backstory. I do like to have a kind of a backstory for a character that I can allow to inform my performance. So I used them quite well. They had really good specialists who you could always go to and ask.
	
		What was the make-up situation like to get Thrain’s nose and beard on?	

	The whole team were amazing. They were getting at like 2 in the morning. I’m getting around 3 and sometimes you’d have to be ready on set about 7.30. So there were 4 1/2 hours of makeup. I meditate today and my meditation stretches to 40 minutes. So I’d have a 40 minutes meditation and come out my meditation with a big nose and big ears. 

	One of my fears of doing something with such big makeup was that the performances would have to be big. I’m not a very big performative actor. It’s not something I’m comfortable with. And then I began watching and working with Owain and Sophie [Nomvete], and I saw that their performances were so natural — not minimalistic, but free. They weren’t pushing it too hard. I realized that I could sit in and relax and just act it like anything else, and it would come through because the makeup was so good. So within the first week, I suddenly felt really comfortable.
	
		This show’s in its third season. How was it joining something when it’s kind of already so far in? 	

	It was great, because I already knew so many people. Kevin Eldon is an old friend of mine. And Owain and I had workshopped a theater piece years ago. I’ve been a big fan of his for years. And Paul Hickey was in it, playing one of the villains I think. I’ve been in the game so long so I turn up and know everyone. I also knew half the crew. The makeup designer — knew her when she was a young girl because she’s the niece of Peter King, who designed the makeup for Lord of the Rings, and he’s my daughter’s godfather. So that’s what I mean. It was part of our life, really. I was connected to it before I joined this series.
	
		Given that “Lord of the Rings” has been a part of your family’s life for so long, if you’d have been able to pick any character to play, who would it have been? Would it have been a dwarf?	

	I think I would have liked maybe to play one of the Hobbits. I think they were great. I ended up subsequently working with a lot of those actors. But Thrain is a great character, he really is. It was a great joy to play him.

title: Jimmy Kimmel Calls for Donald Trump to Resign Amid Republicans’ Midterm Elections Losses: ‘Quit Already … Nobody Wants You’
description: Jimmy Kimmel predictably roasted U.S. President Donald Trump and the Republican party in his late-night monologue on Wednesday following the Democr
body:
Jimmy Kimmel predictably roasted U.S. President Donald Trump and the Republican party in his late-night monologue on Wednesday following the Democrats’ big win in the midterm elections. 

	In what’s been coined a “blue wave,” the Democratic party took control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in Tuesday’s elections, and also flipped governorships in Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Georgia. After celebrating the victory, Kimmel turned to Trump and his claim that if he were on the ballot, the Republicans would have won more races.
	

	“That is such crap,” Kimmel responded. “You were on the ballot. You’re like dog hair; you’re on everything. You’ve infected every nook and cranny of our lives. You divided this country like no one else ever divided it before. The only time you ever brought us together was yesterday, when we all teamed up to get rid of you!” 

	Pointing out Trump’s own changes between political parties over the years, Kimmel said that he “has no allegiance to anyone or anything” and the “only party he leads is the slumber party.”

	“The verdict is in, and there’s only one thing left for Nappy Gilmore to do: Resign,” Kimmel said. “Quit already, just quit. Nobody wants you. Even you don’t want to be president anymore. Take that billion dollars worth of crypto, buy an island. Maybe Epstein’s island? Wouldn’t that be a perfect end to this story!”

	Kimmel then took the time to acknowledge a statement the White House put out about him in response to his monologue on the eve of the elections. “Jimmy Kimmel is a no-talent loser who has beclowned himself with tanking ratings and by spewing disgusting lies to his dwindling audience,” the statement from White House spokesperson Danny Ingle reads. “He is so devoid of actual talent that nobody with any common sense would ever watch him unless it was to laugh at him.”
	

	Kimmel fired back: “Which is kind of the point of the show, but apparently I’ve beclowned myself once again. And that, by the way, almost word-for-word the same statement they’ve issued about me two times in the past year. I got a third beclowned, which I think is the last warning.”

	But Kimmel delivered the ultimate zinger when referring to being called a “no-talent loser,” saying: “The last thing I want to do is tell you how to do your job, Danny Dingle, but today seems like a bad day for you to call me a loser.”

	Watch Kimmel’s full monologue below.
